sections.h2: What to know before selling in Lower Providence Township
sections.html:
Lower Providence is a Montgomery County suburb of about 25,600 residents, in the Perkiomen Creek valley, and includes the Audubon and Evansburg areas. Every sale needs a township resale certificate, three account certifications and a 1 percent local transfer tax. Those four items drive your schedule, and sellers who start them early finish sooner.

An agent listing, a sale by owner and an as-is cash purchase all trigger the same township paperwork, covered below.

The Methacton School District serves the township, and school boundaries are a common question from out-of-area buyers. Arrowhead, Eagleville and Woodland elementary schools take students from different sections, and Skyview Upper Elementary and Arcola Intermediate sit inside the township. Methacton High School is across the line in Worcester Township.

Commuters look first at U.S. Route 422, the Pottstown Expressway, which crosses the southern part of the township. Route 363 handles local trips along Trooper Road, Ridge Pike and Park Avenue. SEPTA suburban buses 91, 93, 99 and 131 connect to the Norristown Transportation Center. Nearby Evansburg State Park and Mill Grove make useful listing details. Mention the elementary school zone and the distance to the Route 422 ramps, since commuters and families ask about both before they book a showing.

Sellers need a residential resale use and occupancy certificate. The township charges $100 for it, which covers the first inspection and one follow-up visit. Re-inspections cost $50 each, starting with the third. The application goes through the township's online permit portal, and residential resale fees are due when the application is filed.

The township finance office also expects tax, sewer and trash accounts to be certified before settlement. The real estate tax certification costs $25 and comes from the elected tax collector. Sewer fees are handled by the sewer authority on Parklane Drive in Eagleville, and trash service is billed by J. P. Mascaro and Sons.

For questions on the inspection, call the Community Development Department at 610-635-3512. The office takes calls on weekdays and returns voicemail left after hours the next business day.

The realty transfer tax on a Lower Providence sale is 2 percent in total: 1 percent to the Commonwealth and 1 percent local. The local share is divided evenly, one half of a percent to the township and one half to the Methacton School District. The state holds buyer and seller liable together, and most contracts divide the cost between them.

A few recurring tax facts matter at the closing table:

  • The township's 2026 real estate levies are 2.1298 mills for the general fund, 0.3727 for the library, 0.7485 for debt service, 0.7614 for emergency services and 0.241 for parks, which together equal 4.2534 mills. County and Methacton school taxes are billed in addition.
  • Tax bills go out on March 1. Payment before April 30 earns a 2 percent discount, and a 10 percent penalty applies after July 1.
  • When your lender pays taxes out of escrow, send each bill along to the lender.

Deeds between certain relatives and property that passes by inheritance can be exempt from the state tax. Before signing, ask the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds what paperwork proves the exemption.

sections.h2: Can I appeal my Montgomery County assessment before I sell?
sections.html:
Yes. Annual appeals go to the Montgomery County Board of Assessment Appeals, which accepts them through August 1 by postmark. It will not take a fax or an email.

For a single-family house the processing fee is $50, payable to the county treasurer, and you send three copies of your evidence, for example an appraisal, comparable sales or photographs. All appeals must be heard by October 31, and the board grants rescheduling only in extraordinary circumstances. A homestead or farmstead appeal costs nothing. The board's office phone is 610-278-3761.

A lower assessment helps the next owner more than the seller, but a documented appeal can still support a price discussion with a buyer.

sections.h2: Selling when you are behind on property taxes
sections.html:
Township, school and county taxes that go unpaid are handed to the Montgomery County Tax Claim Bureau. If taxes from two years back are still owed, the Bureau can sell the parcel. Its upset sales are held each September and December. Whoever buys at an upset sale inherits every lien on the property, whereas a judicial sale delivers it free and clear.

Settle a delinquency before it reaches that stage. Selling before the bureau acts lets the closing pay the arrears from proceeds. Call the bureau at the Norristown office to confirm the payoff figure before you accept an offer.

Begin at the township. Submit the resale certificate application through the online permit portal and pay the filing fee. Fix anything the inspector flags, because a failed visit means a follow-up, and the third re-inspection onward costs extra. Request the tax certification from the elected tax collector, and ask the sewer authority and the trash hauler for their account certifications.

Once an offer is accepted, the title company handles the numbers. It splits the tax bill by days of ownership, totals any payoff and lists both transfer tax shares on the settlement statement. Tell your escrow lender about the sale so that account closes cleanly. Afterward the deed is recorded at the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds. Hold on to every certificate, since the buyer's lender can ask to see them.

sections.h2: Cash offer or listing: how to choose
sections.html:
Three things decide it: how fast you must move, what repairs the house needs and how much certainty you want. A listing reaches more buyers, but it brings showings, repair requests after the buyer's inspection and loan contingencies. Cash buyers rarely have a lender to please, so your preferred closing date usually works.

  • Find out which party books and pays for the township resale inspection, and write it into the contract.
  • Weigh each offer by what you keep after the 2 percent transfer tax, any payoff and your share of the certification costs.
  • Confirm that the buyer will accept the house with its current sewer, trash and tax accounts settled at closing.

Start the township certificates the day you decide to sell, since they are the one piece of the sale fully in your hands.

faqs.q: Does Lower Providence Township require an inspection when I sell?
faqs.a: Yes. A residential sale needs a resale use and occupancy certificate. It costs $100, with an initial inspection and one follow-up visit included, and you apply online through the township permit portal.

faqs.q: How much is the transfer tax on a Lower Providence home sale?
faqs.a: It totals 2 percent of the value transferred. Pennsylvania takes 1 percent, and the other 1 percent stays local, divided between the township and the Methacton School District. The county recorder collects when the deed is filed.

faqs.q: Which school district serves Lower Providence?
faqs.a: Methacton School District. Arrowhead, Eagleville and Woodland elementary schools serve parts of the township, and Methacton High School is in neighboring Worcester Township.

faqs.q: When are Lower Providence property tax bills due?
faqs.a: Bills are mailed March 1. Paying before April 30 earns a 2 percent discount, and a 10 percent penalty applies to payments made after July 1.

faqs.q: When is the Montgomery County assessment appeal deadline?
faqs.a: August 1 every year. Your form, three copies of supporting papers and a $50 check for a single-family home all need a postmark or delivery by that day.
